utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone as well. Mr. Tieger, are you -- no. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to continue the cross-examination of witness Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll ask the usher to escort Mr. Neskovic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Yes. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, you'll remember that last -- or yesterday afternoon when we adjourned, I had put a question to you which you had responded by saying it was a very difficult and complex question. You were therefore given yesterday afternoon and overnight to have a think about it. But it's sensible perhaps just to remind you specifically of the question. It was this: By the time we got to late 1991 and early 1992, such instructions or directions as went down to the municipal level of the SDS, did such instructions or directions come from Dr. Karadzic as the president of the party, or from the Main Board, or from the Executive Board, or some mixture, or from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Instructions issued to the local organisations arrived in the way that I have already mentioned when we discussed Variant A and B and the way in which these plans were distributed. There was direct communication between the Municipal Boards and functionaries, with President Karadzic in the form of Variant A and B. And subsequent contact was also possible when people came from the field to see Dr. Karadzic. So people could also see him in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems not to be an answer to your question, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That had struck me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Neskovic, it's clearly asked to you: Instructions or directions as went down to the municipal level of the SDE [sic] -- I took it, Mr. Stewart, you're talking about the instructions or directions that the witness would bring to the lower levels. Is that correct or is it a wrong understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, to clarify, well, the witness or anybody else for that matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if you or anyone else would have to convey any instructions or directions to the municipal level, from whom did you or did the others receive instructions to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not issue instruction or directives during that period of time, as I have already said. I mentioned the sort of work I had to do. I didn't convey instructions of any kind or directives of any kind. I think that the Municipal Boards acted in accordance with the instructions from Variant A and B and in various manners and they had contact with Karadzic, whom they would visit. As far as I am concerned, I didn't play a role of any kind when it came to conveying instructions or orders. No specific secret couriers were used or representatives or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, perhaps -- Mr. Neskovic, I'll put this to you, then: Are you saying that apart from the Variant A and B instructions, as you put it, that you were not yourself aware of any instructions, directions, or guidelines given to municipalities from the higher levels of the party in late 1991 and early 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's always -- it's my fault perhaps, Mr. Neskovic. There's always an ambiguity with yes or nos. You are saying you agree with what I just put to you, are you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was familiar with instructions -- or rather, the instructions contained in Variant A and B. That's what I was familiar with, although I had not received those instructions. I didn't have them on me. As to what municipal functionaries discussed with Dr. Karadzic when they went to see him, I really don't know. I wasn't present and I didn't issue instructions of any kind. So that's why I know nothing about that, because I wasn't involved in that kind of work. And there's nothing more I can tell you about that, because I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I'm on the record there as saying there's always an ambiguity with yes or no. I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- I mean anything as sweeping as that. But Your Honour sees what I meant in the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I'd like to know: You told us that you visited quite a lot of municipalities and would speak with the SDS people over there. Who did send you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I usually went when the Main Board took such a decision or the Executive Board, and sometimes it was at the proposal of Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So Mr. Karadzic asked you to go there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In some cases, yes. For example, when there was a problem in the municipality of Modrica, in some cases Karadzic sent me there too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say in some cases it was Karadzic. In the other cases, who sent you in the other cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were decisions taken by the Main Board or by the Executive Board. There were conclusions according to which a certain representative should go into the field in order to resolve a certain problem there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So sometimes it was Mr. Karadzic who asked you to go there and sometimes it was on the basis of decisions by the Main Board and the Executive Board, and your task, then, was to resolve problems at the local level.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, you -- you must have had quite a lot of discretion yourself as to when and in what circumstances you visited a municipality to solve problems. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had a certain amount of freedom. And when I arrived in a certain municipality, I could carry out the task assigned to me in my own way, by using my own method. But as to acting independently in the municipalities, no, that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I think perhaps we're at cross-purposes here, Mr. Neskovic. What I'm putting to you is that on a significant number of occasions the decision to visit a municipality to solve whatever problems there were there was a decision that you could take yourself, without any need to refer to higher authority at all. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you always had, before you visited a municipality -- you always had to get some sort of clearance or approval from a higher level, did you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if there was a problem in a municipality - I mentioned this yesterday - then this problem would be discussed at the Main and Executive Board, and then I would be sent there as a representative in order to deal with the problem. When dealing with the problem, I was able to deal with it in my own way. I would then submit a report. But I never went anywhere on my own initiative. I never tried to deal with any such problems on my own initiative. I always carried out the tasks assigned to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you waited, then, did you, until the next meeting of the Main or the Executive Board before getting approval for you to visit a municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to the statute, I did not have the right to visit municipalities and implement my own policies there. I was a member of a collective body, such as the Main and Executive Board, and it was not for me to act as a maverick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never received any instruction from Mr. Krajisnik to visit a municipality, did you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Krajisnik was not a member of the Executive Board. He was only a member of the Main Board. As far as I can remember, as far as my visits to municipalities are concerned, I never discussed these matters with Krajisnik. Krajisnik didn't have the right to discuss such matters with me. He was only one of the 45 members of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, Mr. Krajisnik had no -- himself had no executive authority over you at all, did he?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At page 25 of Monday's transcript - don't trouble about the page reference yourself, please, Mr. Neskovic - page 25, I guess it will be 24 on Mr. Tieger's, there's a long answer from you that begins: "Yes, I would just like to provide you with a brief explanation." Mr. Neskovic, I think there is no need for you to -- to look at any piece of paper at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, if there's any -- if you would feel any need, please address me and ask whether you can consult any papers. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you say is that -- in the middle of that answer - I'm trying not to skip any relevant context - but you say after the elections -- and you're talking about the multiparty elections in November 1990 -- Dr. Karadzic "didn't pay as much attention to the Main and Executive Board; he focussed on members of executive and legislative power who had assumed state positions on behalf of the SDS. He had far more intense contact with Plavsic and Koljevic, as members of the Presidency, and with Krajisnik, as the president of the Assembly, with eight Serbian ministers who are in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He had more contact with functionaries in the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina who are acting on behalf of the SDS." First of all, Mr. Neskovic, can we take it that your -- your knowledge of such matters was largely a matter of impression, rather than any personal involvement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know about that is that after the elections, the party became marginal in a certain sense when it cake to decision-making. Mr. Karadzic and Krajisnik and others who were part of the executive power structure had the most power to take decisions, as far as I know, on the basis of conversations, on the basis of their contact. Well, I know very little about their discussions, their contacts, et cetera, because I wasn't present when Karadzic discussed matters with various Serbian representatives in the executive power structure, so I really don't know what they discussed. I can only say that I stand by my position that Karadzic focussed more on representatives in power and after the elections, the party -- parties became in a certain sense marginalised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that when you talk about Dr. Karadzic having more contact with functionaries in the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina who are acting on behalf of the SDS, that you were not yourself personally involved in any contact with those functionaries in the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred - and this was page 28 of my transcript of Monday - an answer beginning -- an answer from you beginning, "Well, yes, it's a fact." And about 15 lines down in that answer, you say that you and others "believed that Mr. Krajisnik had become the president of the Assembly not thanks to his work within the party but thanks to his personal relationship with Karadzic." Do you recall that there was also, Mr. Neskovic - I should make clear and to the Trial Chamber I'm not -- not challenging that particular point about personal relationship - but do you recall that there was also a question of Mr. Krajisnik being a suitable geographical compromise candidate in the sense that he was living in Sarajevo but he originally came from the Krajina and that was a positive point, in favour of his taking that position? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Krajisnik was Mr. Karadzic's personal choice. And I think that the candidate before him for the post of president of the Assembly was Mr. Trbojevic, who's a lawyer from Sarajevo, but Karadzic, for reasons that are familiar to him, decided to choose Krajisnik and he intervened to ensure that Krajisnik became the president of the Assembly. The geographical reasons you mentioned I think are irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, are you saying that you -- you don't know about those geographical reasons, or you positively assert that they didn't come into the equation?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that geographical factors played a significant role at the time. There was a tendency towards centralisation and most of the functionaries in the executive power and in the MUP came from Sarajevo. So geographical factors were represented in certain constituencies alone. I'm not aware of the fact that after the elections in 1990 geographical factors played a role of any kind when it comes to the executive bodies, such as the government, the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, and other governmental bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Neskovic, you -- well, no, let me put this to you: In fact Mr. Krajisnik was a good choice for that position, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. That was Mr. Karadzic's opinion. Others believed that Mr. Trbojevic would be a good choice, since he was a lawyer, and they believed that it would be appropriate to have a lawyer as the president of the Assembly. Mr. Krajisnik was a financial manager, so it was Radovan's opinion that Mr. Krajisnik was the best choice for that post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put the question -- it's a slightly different point I had in mind. As it turned out, Mr. Krajisnik was a good choice, wasn't he? He was good in that position.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you clarify your question. Are you asking me for my personal opinion about that or are you asking for a general assessment?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking for your -- if you say you don't know enough to -- to answer the question, then that would be a helpful answer, Mr. Neskovic. I'm asking -- I'm putting it to you from your observation of the work of the SDS and the Assembly, such as you were able to observe that, do you agree that Mr. Krajisnik turned out to be a good choice and was good at that job?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the point of view of Mr. Karadzic's policies, from the point of view of his vision and his overall view of the situation, there is no doubt that Krajisnik was a good choice. He suited Mr. Karadzic and his ideas. As to whether Mr. Krajisnik was a good choice generally speaking for that post, I couldn't say. There are various opinions and I could not really provide you with a good answer. From the point of view of Mr. Karadzic's politics, Krajisnik was the best choice for the position of president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, at the turn of the year 1991 to 1992 - right? So we're talking about 31st December 1991, 1st of January, 1992 - where did you disagree with Dr. Karadzic's policies?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not sure whether I disagreed with his policies. I can't remember having any clashes. But there was a large group that did not agree with certain personnel policies because Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik often visited party bodies when it came to personnel policies and they would appoint individuals to posts in executive power structures and they didn't ask the party bodies, such as the Main Board. Out of eight ministers in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were representing the SDS, there was only one who was a prominent SDS member, and that was Mr. Ostojic, whereas the other seven were the personal choice of Mr. Karadzic and of his associates. They were not active members of the SDS. In the MUP, there were no active SDS members. The personnel in the MUP were also personally chosen by Mr. Karadzic. As to the extent to which Krajisnik participated in such matters with Karadzic, I really don't know. That's something that the two of them know. So this is where there was a disagreement, because there were a lot of people involved in executive power on behalf of the SDS, whereas the Main Board of the SDS and even the personnel committee of the SDS had no say in such matters, or if anyone asked them about such matters, it would only be after decisions had already been taken. And it's in that sense that there was a disagreement with Mr. Karadzic. Secondly, there was a disagreement because of the fact that Mr. Karadzic frequently went to Belgrade and came back to us with directives from Milosevic. They wanted to know why we always had to listen to Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, with His Honour's permission, I wonder if I might interrupt you there because I did ask you where you disagreed with Dr. Karadzic's policies, and I wasn't asking you to tell the Court where everybody else disagreed and all about Belgrade and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I -- okay. I think the witness needs some room for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Latitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I understood him to be answering the question in just that way. I mean, if there is a distinction between the disagreements he's outlining in his own view, He can certainly clarify that. But I certainly understood him to be talking about disagreements with those policies that he shared -- or disagreements that he shared. But that can be clarified. But I certainly understood him to be answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I -- in a sense, I'm not too fussed. It's just that I -- I don't want the 60 per cent guideline to be applied if my questions are treated as a free range for the witness to explore such issues as he feels are relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, the same happened when he was answering questions from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may interrupt him if he goes away from your question, and I would not mind, but in this particular instance, I think he was answering the question, although in a perhaps bit different way. Where you asked him whether he disagreed with the policies, he described in what way he disagreed with the personnel policy as was conducted by Mr. Karadzic and that is, although an indirect answer, relevant for your question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say in relation to -- if Your Honour is suggesting some sort of equation, one should subtract such answers --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I say this, please. That one should subtract from the Prosecution time for purposes of calculations in the same way one should subtract from the Defence. They are not symmetrical because long answers given during the course of Prosecution evidence are material on which I would therefore need to consider cross-examination and to cross-examine -- cross-examine accordingly. But, Your Honour, when it comes to my time, if the witness is straying into areas which are not what I am looking for, not what I am asking him about, then it is fundamentally unfair to count that in any way as part of the allocation of calculation in relation to cross-examination, because as far as I am concerned, it is not part of my cross-examination; it's a frolic of the witness's own into areas which I didn't ask him about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You expressed your opinion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I expressed my submission, Your Honour. My opinions I generally keep to myself, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, to the extent that the witness has -- went into many details totally irrelevant for the Prosecution's case, I do not think that there will be any need to cross-examine the witness on those irrelevant, non-assisting parts of his answers. But let's proceed at this moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I'm not reviving my previous question. I'm going on to page 29 of your transcript of your evidence on Monday, which -- the point -- it's the first long paragraph of your answer. The second paragraph begins: "So it was a very important position." If that's the reference point. And a few lines above that, you said: "So the president of the Municipality" -- and that was that translation issue when I was otherwise engaged, Your Honour. But it's completely obvious and we're all agreed, Mr. Tieger and I, that it should say "Assembly." So the president of the Assembly "in the former system of Bosnia and Herzegovina," the president of the Assembly, "has an extremely important position because this involves legislative power, constitutional power, executive power." Mr. Neskovic, the phrase "executive power," what executive power did the position of president of the Assembly in the former system of Bosnia and Herzegovina give to the holder?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about two things here, if I may. The president of the Assembly and the former -- in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina is one thing and the president of the Assembly of the Republika Srpska is quite another. We are talking about two separate political systems and things are rather different there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I'm going to stop you, please, with respect, there because what we are actually talking about, with respect, is what my question is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's -- Mr. Stewart, if you'd look at the transcript, I think your question is not transcribed as you put it to the witness. Perhaps you could repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you said what executive power in the constitutional system was given to the holder of the office of the president of the Assembly. I think that's what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, Your Honour. That's what it says, at line 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- yes, but I think you referred to the constitutional system. And here the question - please read it again - now it says: "What executive power did the president of the Assembly in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina give to the holder?" That's certainly not what you meant to ask and it's also not my recollection that that's what you asked him. I mean, as we read it now, it says if what executive power the president of the Assembly gave to the holder of the office of the president of the Assembly, which doesn't make that much sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you referred to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, tremendous confusion is being produced. It's quite likely that the word "president" in that line should simply be Presidency, which would make the whole thing clear. Your Honour, in case my -- in case my question as a combination of the transcript, Your Honour's observations, my question is now confusing, it's better if I simply put it very clearly to the witness and indicate to him what the constraints of my question are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think, as a matter of fact, Mr. Stewart, that what I did is to serve the interest of the Defence here where the question did not appear properly on the transcript. And, of course, you are invited to put the question to the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that would serve the interest of the Defence now. Thank you for Your Honour's assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I'm not asking you in this next question about Presidency of the Assembly of Republika Srpska or the Serb republic. I'm not asking you about that. This question relates to the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, when it was a multi-national Assembly. You said in your own evidence that the -- that position involved legislative power, constitutional power, executive power. And my question is: What executive power did that position give to its holder?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for your help. I hope that's clear now.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what I said, because I -- if that's what I said, I must admit I must have made a mistake, because the president of the Assembly in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina had no executive powers. He had the following authority: To convene the meetings of the Assembly, to propose the agenda for those meetings, and on the basis of his authority, he could influence the make-up of different commissions and committees, such as for defence, security, et cetera. And on the basis of his capacity, he was a member of the constitutional committee and on the basis of that and together with the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, he was a part of the top leadership of the state, also with respect to any emergency or special circumstances. And I think he would have also been a member of some kind of top command or defence council or something like that. So in the old system of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina the president of the Assembly was a role which was something that you had to reckon with with regard to developing any policies of the state. And also there was an extra role: He would have been a secretary of the central committee and then was the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the president of the Assembly, the president of the government, the head of government, and those people made up the top political leadership. In the former system of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is indeed true that they did not have any direct executive powers, but this president was nevertheless a member of the top body at the state level and he had a certain level of control over the executive branch of the authority that -- of power - that is to say, the government - through either the MPs club or the committee for the control of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I have to ask you to slow down because the French translation is already a couple of lines behind. Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I also just observe this: Your Honour, again, it's not -- it's for me to request but not in the end to restrict. This answer is straying to the very edges of my question and Your Honours will be aware that we have had in the course of the last year and a half an enormous amount of evidence explaining the structures and the basic positions that people held. And this witness to be adding to that is not, in my submission, is not actually assisting, But it's Your Honours' judgement there, assisting the Trial Chamber in gathering the evidence and the facts in relation to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least the witness corrected his testimony to the extent that where he said that he had executive powers, that under the system he had not -- and then he started describing the influence -- the influential positions the speaker of the Assembly might have had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first -- the first bit was directly an answer to my question and is certainly of extreme valuable assistance to the Trial Chamber. That's why I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm thinking of where we got to now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I said at least the witness at the very beginning - but I didn't add that - corrected his testimony to the extent that where he said that he had executive powers, that under the system he had not. So I fully acknowledge both the correction the witness made to his earlier testimony and the importance of it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm 100 per cent agreeing with Your Honour about that. But it doesn't mean the question should be allowed -- the answer should be allowed to go on forever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not -- no, I'm not -- I would not intervene if you would have stopped the witness halfway his explanation, if you did not want to ask him what -- in what other ways he might not have had any influence. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm inviting Your Honour's approval since I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- in fact reprimanded a few minutes ago for stopping the witness. I really do no know where I am, Your Honour. If I stop the witness I should have carried on; if I don't stop the witness, I'm told I should have stopped him. I have to invite Your Honour to take the decision as to when and where to stop the witness, because frankly I give up on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have the approval -- and you're invited to slow down for the purposes of the record. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I -- I'm glad the witness had an opportunity to answer the question. In my submission, the witness attempted as rigorously as possible to focus --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not comment on the answer of the witness. The witness started to answer the question. Then further elaborated on matters which are, well, let's say in the margin of the question but not anything more. And I gave Mr. Stewart the approval to stop the witness at this moment and ask his next question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I just wanted to say they thought it was directly within the purview of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So there's some disagreement on that. You may proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm very much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, this next question relates to the Bosnian Serb Assembly. Do you say that Mr. Krajisnik had more executive power as the president of the Bosnian Serb and Republika Srpska Assembly than he had had as the president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Except we should drop the term "executive." He had greater powers and was more powerful all round as president of the Assembly of the Bosnian Serbs than he had in Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to stop you straight away because I'm afraid Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it's not in your prerogative to drop the "executive" which was in my question. You are not entitled, Mr. Neskovic, with respect, to rephrase my question and answer the question you wish to answer. You used the phrase "executive power" in your evidence and corrected yourself in relation to the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I asked you questions which you answered fully on the -- the answer to whether is there was executive power in the president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I am now asking you about executive power of Mr. Krajisnik in relation to the Assembly -- the Serb Assembly. You did not express, if I may just remark this as an introduction -- you did not express any doubts or difficulties about understanding that phrase when you answered the questions in relation to that Assembly. So I am now asking you with reference to executive power: Do you say that Mr. Krajisnik had greater executive power as the president of the Bosnian Serb Assembly than he had had as president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Do you say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems there was -- Mr. Tieger intended to object. The witness answered the question. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your answer is yes. Please explain where and how.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb Assembly, the Assembly of the Serb Bosnia and Herzegovina, was a central compact body headed by Mr. Krajisnik. That Assembly was not just one in a whole range of other institutions. It was the central body and the moving force behind all the other institutions, and they actually set up all the other institutions, such as the Council of Ministers, and they also made the decision about the setting-up of the Republika Srpska and the Constitution and the judicial system and the courts and the army and the army commanders and the National Security Council, and it proposed all the amendments to all of that. So the entire political system and the entire institutional structure is the baby of that Assembly, basically, because they created it all. So that Assembly was a central institution which created the entire political and institutional system that followed. In that respect, that Assembly was rather significant and Mr. Krajisnik had greater powers as the president of the Serb Assembly, for the simple reason that it was a single ethnicity that was there, and also he was extremely skilful in creating a compact team, in creating a united front in a very skilful diplomatic way. So at the very centre, at the very core of that body there was Mr. Krajisnik, and in a way he was not just formal president of the Assembly or just one of the members; in a way, he was indeed the leader or the political father of that Assembly. So that Assembly was the central body that created all the other bodies and the political system. That's the way I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, you are moving away from the question. I can imagine, Mr. Tieger, that you'd like to ask some questions rather on the -- the influence and the way in which Mr. Krajisnik may have exercised that position. But as far as the executive power is concerned, the last part of your answer is not any more directly related to that. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. May I put down a marker, Your Honour. That implicit invitation to Mr. Tieger in relation to re-examination, if such matters arise properly out of my cross-examination and don't simply go over ground which really was supposedly covered in chief, well, no doubt that will be legitimate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, His Honour - and I have no quarrel, I should say, with respect - His Honour stopped you at that point. I just want to be clear. That's -- that answer you gave, that's as -- that's as much as you can say about executive power of Mr. Krajisnik, as the president of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, is it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the president of the Assembly, he was not entrusted with any executive authority. It was up to the executive branch, such as the Council of Ministers and at a later stage the government and all the various other bodies in that respect, because there was a division between legislative -- the legislative and the executive branches of authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Neskovic. That was a helpfully succinct answer, if I may say so. The -- Mr. Neskovic, a different topic. And this was around pages 52 through to about 59 on my transcript of Monday's hearing. There was questioning about your application for a loan, and then there were various questions about your contention that people had managed to acquire flats in Belgrade and make money and people being on friendly terms with Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic and so on. I'm going to try, Mr. Neskovic, to reduce this to a very simple question. Mr. Neskovic, could you confirm that you have absolutely no basis of knowledge yourself to suggest that Mr. Krajisnik was ever involved in any unlawful or improper financial dealings in 1991 or 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no evidence of that, and I don't want to engage in guesswork. I have knowledge, as many other citizens do, on the basis of many reports in the media, of quite a few scandals that sent shock waves through the Republika Srpska with regard to government and other bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, do you know that there had been a previous time when Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic had both been on trial together for some alleged illegal financial and fraudulent activities?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They didn't hear your answer, Mr. Neskovic. It was nice and short, I hope.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the result of those legal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were those proceedings for white-collar crimes. It was about a company within the framework of the Energoinvest company and the outcome was a verdict of not guilty from the Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I really don't know how long it took, the entire proceedings, I mean. Between one and three years. But I think the end result was a ruling in favour and I believe that came from the Supreme Court of the BH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you, in fact, recall that the end result was that Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic, for that matter, was completely acquitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it that that's what the verdict of not guilty is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that as far as I know, they were pronounced not guilty of those accusations. That means that they had indeed been acquitted. But the company in question did also go bankrupt and the employees lost their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just didn't see the phrase "not guilty" previously on the transcript. If I've overlooked it, then my apologies. I didn't see it there. That was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I heard it, at least. Whether it's -- perhaps it's not on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it isn't, I think, Your Honour, which is -- and perhaps I didn't hear it either. Well, perhaps the person doing the transcript didn't hear it and is in the same position as me. It doesn't matter, Your Honour. It's -- it is clear, isn't it. I've asked respectfully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, the meeting that you described in December at which you say the Variants A and B document was distributed, do you remember that -- well, first of all, there was to be a -- an Assembly meeting on the 21st of December, wasn't there? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I mean, I don't remember the date, the 21st of December. I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can jog your memory. It was a Saturday, the 21st of December, 1991. There was to be an Assembly meeting on the Saturday. Do you -- can you -- do you remember that, if I jog in that way?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's no big help, because I can't recall that Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, is it correct that the -- the meeting that you refer to, the large meeting -- and I should make it clear, so we understand some basic guidelines. I'm not suggesting there was no meeting of any sort. That's what I'm putting to you. So the large meeting, whatever it was, was fixed for and took place at 4.00 or around 4.00 on the Friday afternoon, which, in fact, was the 20th of December. Now, does that -- do you have a recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think it was the 19th of December, St. Nicholas' Day, at the Holiday Inn. As to the 20th of December, I can't remember that. I think that the meeting was held on the 19th of December. It's the day of St. Nicholas. And that was in the meeting room that I had already mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you keep a diary at the time, Mr. Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never kept a diary or made any notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you went on all these visits to municipalities, they -- they were never recorded in any sort of personal or working diary of your own; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I told here about the municipalities, that was recorded in the minutes of those meetings at the municipalities. And afterwards, I would report back to my authorities higher up, but it was done orally. So there are written records at the municipality level pertaining to that activity of mine, but I myself did not tend to make any notes and I did not have a diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I'm not suggesting it's -- so we've got it clear, you just personally -- it is not your practice to keep a personal diary. That's what you're saying, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no. It would have been more useful had I done that and at the time, I didn't feel it was necessary, so I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, the -- the meeting that I am putting to you took place on the Friday afternoon, do you recall that after you and others arrived in Sarajevo for whatever meeting or meetings were to take place over those few days, that news came through that the European Union, pushed by Germany, the European Union was moving towards recognition of the independence of Croatia and in the direction of approving or recognising independence consequently of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. After the meeting on the 19th of December at that meeting room at the Holiday Inn Hotel, I went home and I did not attend any other meetings afterwards, nor was I involved in any talks in relation to what I -- what you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember, then, Mr. Neskovic, that this move -- Croatia being very significant at that time, that this -- that this move towards what appeared to be accelerated recognition of the independence of Croatia caused considerable consternation among the Serb delegates and representatives who had come to Sarajevo at that time in December? You don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. But I do remember something else perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is it an answer to my question, Mr. Neskovic, what else you remember? Or is it closely relevant?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The secession of Slovenia and Croatia from Yugoslavia did not cause such a huge crisis amongst the public opinion in the BH, not even among the Serbs, because they did that in a constitutional way and over a longer time period of about two years. What was frightening for Serbs - that is to say, their representatives, politicians, and the people, the public opinion - was the possibility of Bosnia and Herzegovina going for independence and being recognised as an independent state internationally. That did cause fear and bitterness. But as to Slovenia and Croatia, they proceeded in a fully constitutional way, in line with the international law, and it went over a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I think perhaps I could cut this short. It's a phrase used in a slightly different context in relation to a different conflict, but there was a sort of domino concern, wasn't there, that -- Mr. Neskovic, to make it clear, I'm not putting to you that the central concern of you and your colleagues was Croatia, Slovenia, but it was this, wasn't it, in a nutshell: There was deep concern and consternation that recognition of independence of Croatia and Slovenia increased significantly the prospect of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and -- well, that's -- that's -- let's take it in stages. That's true, as far as it goes, isn't it, Mr. Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. When Slovenia and Croatia were internationally recognised, there were intensive negotiations being conducted between representatives of the Serbs and Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Belgrade also acted as a player. I think this was in August 1991, and I think they were trying to reach a Serbian and Muslim historical agreement. Bosnia-Herzegovina would remain within Yugoslavia as part of that agreement and Izetbegovic would become its first president. This agreement almost succeeded. At the time, there were Muslim and Serb negotiations about a historical agreement between the Serbs and the Muslims. I think that Koljevic, Adil -- and Adil Zulfikarpasic was involved. I think it was in August 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, let's -- let's put on one side, if one can, Croatia and Slovenia. The news had filtered through at the time of this gathering in Sarajevo that the European Community, I think it was called then -- the European Community had raised with the Bosnia and Herzegovina government directly the question of whether it wished to proceed towards independence. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think so that is what happened. I think there was some document from the European Community. Perhaps it concerned a meeting in The Hague or somewhere else. And it was said that all the republics in Yugoslavia would be recognised if they met certain criteria. So international recognition concerned all the republics, as far as I am aware.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Neskovic, it was that issue, among others, but that was a very important issue which led to the meeting on the Friday being more heavily attended by a wider range of people than had originally been planned. Do you have any recollection as to whether what I've just put to you is right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that meeting. I can't even remember whether I attended it or not. So there's nothing I could tell you about that. I can't make any guesses if I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So which meeting do you say you can't remember if you attended? The ...?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting at which they discussed the possibility of Europe for recognising the independence of Slovenia and Croatia. I can only remember the meeting at which Variant A and B were discussed, but the meeting where international policies and international recognition were subjects that were discussed, I can't remember that meeting or perhaps I have forgotten it. But I can't remember having attended it and there's nothing I can tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there was any large meeting held in Sarajevo of Bosnian Serbs over that three- or four-day period that you didn't attend? Sorry, tell me if that's not clear, Mr. Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a meeting. I think it was a meeting of Serbian intellectuals or a session of Serbian intellectuals or something like that. That's what it was called. There was one such meeting held in the Holiday Inn. There were a lot of Serbian intellectuals from Bosnia and Herzegovina and beyond who attended it. And at that meeting, they discussed these various issues, and perhaps they discussed this issue too. I did not attend this meeting and I do not know what they discussed there. The meeting of Serbian intellectuals was held there and there was a significant number of them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, you have described in your evidence how Dr. Karadzic in a fairly formal, structured way distributed a number of copies of the Variant A and B document. You recall your evidence on that, do you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it -- it was about -- what was it? Was it about 100 copies, 50? What -- you said there were 200 people at the meeting. How many, roughly, copies did Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic hand out in that fashion?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 200 people attended the meeting. Fewer people were given copies. I can't remember how many. He distributed the number of copies that were necessary for Serbs, for presidents of municipalities. I'm not quite sure how many copies were distributed. There were perhaps around 100 copies that were distributed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it -- was it something like this, Mr. Neskovic, that something like 100 individuals walked up to the front table and received their copy of Variants A and B from Dr. Karadzic? Was it like that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Karadzic called out individuals who were on a list. I think that some approached the desk and took their copies and in some cases perhaps it was their assistant or the secretary who provided them with a copy. But on the whole, they approached the desk, took those copies from Karadzic, and as far as I can remember - but I'm not certain about this - they were duty-bound to read them and then to return them to Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sure school prize-givings vary around the world, Mr. Neskovic. Was it something -- you make it sound as if it was like a school prize-giving, with -- with people being called up and handed their -- their document and then going back to their seats. Is -- is that what it was like?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not really. Since the documents had been marked "highly confidential," individuals were called out who were allowed to examine this confidential material. So it's not quite as if it resembled prize-giving ceremonies in schools.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What -- do you know that these -- you can see, in fact, from tab 11 -- do you want to have a look at, please -- well, please look at tab 11 in the bundle in front of you. We call them bundles where I come from. Now, you -- you will look at the Serbian version, of course, Mr. Neskovic, and you see it's numbered 93; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What -- what happened if the person being -- well, did it happen occasionally that the person being called up, then, to be handed their copy of Variant A and B was not there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say what happened for sure. I wondered whether Djurovic was present or not, but I thought that if someone was not present, in such cases Karadzic found another way of providing that person with the document. And last night I was asking myself whether Djurovic was present and whether he personally collected a copy of the document. This happened a long time ago, and I can't remember who was present, but most of those concerned by the document were present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the handing-out of these copies of Variant A and B by Dr. Karadzic take? You can put the document aside, I think.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, as usual, Karadzic, as the leader, first gave some kind of introductory speech that had to do with the position of the Serbs, the threat the Serbs were under --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Neskovic, I'm not asking about that. I -- my question is a very confined one here. I'll put it a different way. From the moment when Dr. Karadzic handed out the first copy of Variant A and B to the moment when he'd handed out the last copy of Variant A and B, how long do you say that process of distribution took?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't take very long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how long would it take 100 people to approach me or you and for us to hand them a document? Well, I don't know, but I think it was done very rapidly. You were just given the document and then you leave. Then the following person comes, and so on and so forth. So it was all done very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, you ask a question and normally counsel, of course, declines to answer questions, but it does give rise to this. I'm going to put a specific suggestion to you to see whether you agree. There you were, 200 of you, sitting in rows; correct? Please stop looking at the document for the moment, Mr. Neskovic, because the document's really got nothing at all now to do with the questions I'm asking you. So if you could just close the file and put it on one side, then you'll be able to concentrate 100 per cent, please, on the questions you're being asked. Well, I'll give it to you again, Mr. Neskovic. First of all, there you were, about 200 of you, sitting in rows of chairs, facing the top table; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, we've all, I take it -- everybody here has been at some sort of physical meeting like that. When people have to stagger along rows from the middle of the row or the end of the row and clamber over other people, Mr. Neskovic, you can't distribute a document like this to 100 people at a meeting like that in less than about half an hour or 45 minutes, can you? Think about it, Mr. Neskovic, and answer as best and clearly and truthfully as you can manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is invited, if it's suited Your Honour, to think about it over the break. I don't mind. I'm entirely in Your Honour's hands if he wishes to have more time to think about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember how much time it took, Mr. Neskovic? Did it take 10 minutes, 20 minutes, 30 minutes, 40 minutes? If you don't remember -- it's a matter -- if it is a matter of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- please. If it's a matter of reconstructing without a clear memory on how much time it approximately has taken, then it doesn't assist the Chamber that much, but do you have still any memory on how much time it took?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, some people were in the third, fourth, or fifth row. Given the time it took them to stand up and come forward then go back, well, it -- it could have taken about an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're now reconstructing rather than talking from your memory, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Because I can't remember. I don't even have a watch, so I can't remember. I can't provide you with a precise answer. I can only try and guess and reconstruct what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I wonder if you would take the -- now the -- the binder or file of documents in front of you and go back to that tab 11, the Variant A and B document. Now, at the very end of that document, in the English version - and of course you'll hear this in translation now anyway, Mr. Neskovic - but in the English version we see typed out as a sort of signature "SDS Crisis Staff," and there's also the original Serbian at the end of the version you're looking at. You told the Court that, if I summarise accurately, that you had no knowledge of there being such a body or organ as the -- the SDS Crisis Staff at the -- the centre. That's -- that's correct, isn't it, Mr. Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you from your knowledge - and if you don't know, please say so - but can you offer any explanation of how it is that Dr. Karadzic would have approved or endorsed the dissemination of a document purportedly coming from a non-existent entity within the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll state once again that there was no SDS Crisis Staff. And as to how Karadzic, as the president of the party, signed on behalf of a non-existent body instead of signing on behalf of himself, well, I can provide you no explanation of that fact. Only Karadzic could provide you with an explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, is it your position that you can positively say that Mr. Krajisnik -- from -- from what you know yourself and what you saw yourself, that Mr. Krajisnik had any knowledge of the contents of this document before it was distributed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was drafted by Mr. Karadzic or brought in by Mr. Karadzic. I don't know whether he had previously informed Mr. Krajisnik of the contents of the document. Krajisnik had the possibility of acquainting himself with the document thanks to his relationship with Karadzic. As to whether he actually drafted this document together with Karadzic or participated in some other way, I really do not know. Yesterday I said that as far as I can remember, Krajisnik sat next to Dr. Karadzic in the Presidency. Mr. Krajisnik had the possibility of seeing this document before it was distributed, but as to whether he actually did that, I do not know, so I cannot answer your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you offer any explanation of how and why Mr. Krajisnik might have approved or endorsed the distribution of a document purportedly coming from the non-existent SDS Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that that's what I said in my answer. I said that Krajisnik and Karadzic represented a supreme body. They took all the decisions together. They informed each other of everything. And given such a situation, I came to the conclusion that it was possible for Krajisnik to familiarise himself with the document. But as to whether he actually did that or not, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I have some problems. You said whether the witness "can offer any explanation how and why Mr. Krajisnik might have approved." It's not established that he approved or endorsed it. He --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's right. That's my pause as I ask that question, was that it contains a -- that hypothetical element precisely because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you're asking how and why something we do not know, what it happened -- well, of course, it calls for a lot of -- it calls for a lot of speculation. But -- well, the witness couldn't anxious the question anyhow, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. I believe I could justify the question. It doesn't matter. I'm not pressing -- well, I don't need to pursue that particular point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- Mr. Neskovic, you cannot say, can you, with any confidence at all that Mr. Krajisnik was present in the room when this Variant A and B document was distributed.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but I think Mr. Krajisnik was in the room and that he was even in the working Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the working Presidency, Mr. Neskovic, at the moment. I'm asking about his physical presence in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, but that may be a confusion on the part of counsel, the reference to the working Presidency in the context of the information provided by this witness is clearly a reference to his physical presence in the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, Mr. Stewart puts it to you that you are not certain about the presence of Mr. Krajisnik at the moment when this document was distributed. That's what he puts to you. Whether you agree with that or not. I think yesterday in your testimony you said -- you told us a few details, but Mr. Stewart puts it to you that you could not be certain about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure that when the document itself was being distributed Mr. Krajisnik was there. Perhaps he left the room or he had perhaps left the room at the time. But Mr. Krajisnik was present during that session, yes. People were coming and going. But I cannot claim for certain that when the document was being distributed Mr. Krajisnik was present, nor can I claim that he assisted in any way when the document was being distributed, because there are many people who were entering the room and leaving the room at all times. So since I cannot quite remember what happened, I can't answer your question precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, can we take it that at least quite a few of the people who were present in that room, apart from those who might have been sitting at the top table, so those in the body of the room, at least quite a few of them were personally known to you before the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a lot of people who knew each other. We all knew each other, the deputies, members of the Political Council and of the Main and Executive Board, many representatives from various municipalities. We all knew each other personally, with the exception of some intellectuals who came from outside, some individuals whom we did not know. Most of the people in the room knew each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if - and it's a hypothetical at the moment, Mr. Neskovic - if you were asked to jot down the names of people that you definitely remember being at that meeting, roughly how many names do you -- do you say you would be able to write down?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd write down the names of those in the Executive Committee, the main committee, the entire deputy council, the POLITICAL COUNCIL, Serbian representatives of municipalities, Serbian representatives of Executive Boards, probably certain other regional SDS functionaries, certain intellectuals. How many of them could I mention? Well, out of the 200 individuals present, I believe that I could name at least 100 or 150 people that I personally knew from all of these various bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, leaving aside anybody that you might put in top leadership, Dr. Krajisnik -- I'm sorry, Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Koljevic, and so on, could you -- could you just give immediately six names of people that you definitely remember being at that meeting? Any six.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, I cannot try to guess what their names were. I believe that Jovan Cizmovic was there. I believe that Brdjanin was there. Representatives of various Executive Boards and municipality were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Names, Mr. Neskovic --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you any names with certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't name any individuals. That was a long time ago and there were a lot of people there. I could not mention any names. I might mistakenly name someone who was not there. But representatives of most of the bodies that I have mentioned were present. I would not now like to speculate and mention names if I can't really remember these names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, then, Mr. Neskovic, and let's take the file -- well, you've got it. You've got it in front of you. That's helpful. Let's go -- you were asked -- and we're moving on to the transcript of yesterday, the 19th of July. And I don't know how far my page numbering coincides there, but my page 2 starts: "Good morning." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. If Mr. Tieger's page 2 starts "Good morning," then we're in an even happier position than we were on Monday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm able to follow so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. That's all I ask, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were asked in the middle of that page, line 12 on my transcript: "May I ask" -- this was Mr. Tieger asking you: "May I ask you next to turn to tab the 12 and look at item 9." So may I ask you, Mr. Neskovic, to turn to tab 12 and look at item 9. Thank you. Well, actually I realise straight away though that was the introduction. I actually want you to look at item 7. That shouldn't cause a major difficulty. The same page, 23rd of December, tab 12, item 7. Do you see "Responsible" and the four names, Bogdanovic, Nastic, Prijic, Sojic? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then turning over to tab 13, you were asked about item 11. The same four names appear and the task, to provide larger quantities of food and medicaments and to transfer them to a safe location. And you were -- it was put to you by Mr. Tieger that those were essentially the same tasks and the same persons hay signed. And you said: "These tasks" -- this is page 3, line 21 -- "These task do overlap to a certain extent" and you referred to an item which you said was missing. I don't need to go over all that. First of all, Mr. Neskovic, this particular item only covered a part of the ground in the Variant A and B document, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were wondering whether these duties related to Variant A or B, and then when I had a look at the names, I came to the conclusion that it concerned Variant A, and I said that I thought that there was something missing in the document. The name of the Crisis Staff commander is -- is not mentioned, because the duties assigned are very precise for all groups. But then we don't have the name of the commander who assigned these duties. So something is missing in the document but it does relate to Variant A. There's no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we turn back to Variant A - and that's - well, it's page 5 of the English, but I'll have to invite you in tab 11 to find under "first level" -- "Variant A, first level," item number 11 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on page 3 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm obliged. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least, it starts on page 3, going to 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you -- do you see that, witness? Page 3 of the --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And number 11 there, item 11 Variant A first level, it self-contains, do you see --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I may. Maybe this is a quick moment. I just can sense something that's going to require a lot of potential -- perhaps I can mention something to Mr. Stewart when the witness doesn't have his headphones on. I'll certainly leave his examination up to him. But -- up to him. But I don't know if there's any confusion that might be resolved quickly that might pre-empt unnecessary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, do you -- do you speak or understand any English? The reaction -- it appears that he does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Apparently not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't speak or understand any English, Mr. Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't speak English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please take your earphones off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I -- I certainly leave it up to Mr. Stewart as to how he wants to conduct the examination, but the examination-in-chief focussed on the December 23rd minutes and related those items as enumerated to the enumerated items in -- in A and B. That correspondence was the subject of some discussion in the examination-in-chief. When -- when we turned in examination-in-chief to the January document, there was certainly no suggestion that those -- the listing of those items and the numbering of those items related back to Variant A and B, which is why I asked whether number 11 related to number 7 in the document. Again, if that's helpful, please take it on board. Otherwise -- because I would be coming back, of course, to -- to re-ask those questions if we got --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your questioning, the link as far as item 11 on the -- of the 29th of January minutes were mainly related to item 7 of the 23rd of December minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. And there's no suggestion that -- that item 11 in the January document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Relates directly to the A and B.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart. Could you please put your earphones on again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That is helpful, Your Honour, because while I did appreciate that there wasn't suggested to be that correlation, I had, I think, extracted from -- in error from the witness's answer that at some point he was talking about Variant A and B when in fact he -- he wasn't. So that is, in fact, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what I understood --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the link with the A and B document is found in the Crisis Staff meeting 23rd of December, where the items are numbered 6, 7, 8, 9, 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Corresponding to the Variant A.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whereas the other only -- the 11 is not in any way linked to the A and B document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That -- my confusion lies elsewhere. I do -- I understand that. My confusion was when picking a reference to an item 11 out of the witness's evidence and incorrectly supposing that he was at that point talking about the A and B document. However, Your Honour, I -- I nevertheless, in fact, wish to stick with item 11, the very item to which I drew attention in Variant A and B, because I -- I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please put a question in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will. But I appreciate Mr. Tieger's helpfulness there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- item 11 that we were looking at under Variant -- Variant A first level, "carry out preparations to ensure" -- and then we see four items: "The protection of children, pregnant women," et cetera; "replenishment of wartime units according to JNA standards, protection of material, resources of interest to defence," and then fourth item not numbered, but "continuing production and services of vital interest for the defence, resistance and survival of the Serbian people." Now, those items were -- responsibility for item 11 there was allocated on the 23rd of December, 1991, to three people, Mr. Gajevic, Mr. Kovac, and Mr. Salapur [phoen]. Mr. Neskovic, if you have any knowledge of this matter, can you say were all the aspects of item 11 in Variant A first level actually implemented in practice in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. That's why I mentioned the fact that one other document seems to be missing and it should be entitled "The report on implemented activities on the part of those groups," and that document is missing. Even though I do know these people referred to in item 11 and I know their whereabouts and -- at the time and their duties and competencies, and I think that this actually refers to yet another document that had already been mentioned, that is to say, the so-called evacuation of Serb population from threatened areas in case of war. Jovic -- Dobrata [phoen] Jovic was an adversary to Prijic, who was to replace him later on as a president of the party, and Drago Kovac appears as the representative to have Territorial Defence, or some such thing. Zdravko Salapur [phoen] is a party official from the local community Pofalici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- yes.
